title: Cold framing on an ext4 NVMe server reads at half the speed of dd
body:
sufr's measurements of `Framed::open` on a server with Dell enterprise NVMe under ext4 on LVM, reported from its session and read with libsail 0.4.3:

| input | warm | cold |
|---|---|---|
| 90.1 GB, 2.57 M records | 14.4 s, 6.2 GB/s | 60-61 s, 1.5 GB/s |
| 21.5 GB, 100 M records | 5.7 s | 16.2 s |
| 19.5 GB, 516 K records | 2.6 s | 13.0 s |
| hg38 without N, 3.1 GB, 455 records | 0.55 s | 2.13 s |

Cold means `posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)` on the file before each run. Plain `dd bs=8M` of the 90 GB file, cold, one run each, read at 2.96 GB/s with one stream and 3.4 to 3.6 GB/s with 4 to 32 streams. Framing warm runs at 6.2 GB/s. That suggests the scan is not what holds the cold read to 1.5 GB/s, though nobody has profiled it. `Framed::map` took the same cold time as `Framed::open`. `read_ahead_kb` is 128 on every block device there.

`Framed::open` builds its index with `build_index`, which reads 64 KiB at a time (`index::CHUNK`).

On an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D with a Samsung 990 PRO, the gap does not reproduce. A cold uncompressed 1 GiB file framed at about 7.4 GB/s, the drive's rated speed, and a plain read with `memchr::memmem` took the same time at 64 KiB, 1 MiB and 8 MiB per read. The harness is `tmp-claude/2026-11-19-fasta-gap/repro/src/floors.rs` in the sail checkout, variants `framed`, `rs64k`, `rs1m` and `rs8m`.

## Proposal

Run those four variants cold on the server before changing anything, together with a variant that calls `posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_SEQUENTIAL)` before reading. If larger reads or the hint close the gap to one `dd` stream, the same change goes into `build_index` and `Reader::fill`.

## Open

- Whether the cause is the read size, the readahead window, or something about LVM on that server.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/0eeac819
notes.text:
Probe results from the server, run by the sufr session with `tmp-claude/2026-11-20-cold-framing-probe` built against libsail 0.4.3. The volume is ext4 mounted `rw,relatime` on an LVM volume over a Dell enterprise NVMe drive, with `read_ahead_kb` 128 on both the LVM device and the drive. The file is 19.46 GB with 515,605 records. Each run is cold, after `posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)`. Times are medians of 3, in seconds.

| variant | time | GB/s |
|---|---|---|
| `Framed::open` | 12.70 | 1.53 |
| `read(2)` 64 KiB plus memmem | 13.20 | 1.47 |
| `read(2)` 64 KiB after `POSIX_FADV_SEQUENTIAL` | 9.59 | 2.03 |
| `read(2)` 1 MiB | 6.61 | 2.94 |
| `read(2)` 8 MiB | 7.38 | 2.64 |
| `read(2)` 8 MiB after `POSIX_FADV_SEQUENTIAL` | 7.38 | 2.64 |
| `index::Reader`, whole file | 7.25 | 2.68 |
| 1 range, one `Reader` | 7.24 | 2.69 |
| 2 ranges | 6.01 | 3.24 |
| 4 ranges | 5.76 | 3.38 |
| `dd bs=8M`, one run | 6.48 | 3.00 |

The read size is the cause. At 64 KiB per read the drive delivers half of what it delivers at 1 MiB, and 1 MiB matches one `dd` stream. The sequential hint recovers part of the gap. `build_index`, under `Framed::open`, reads exactly `index::CHUNK`, which is 64 KiB. `Reader` reads until its buffer is full, and its buffer grows to the longest record, so it already issues larger reads. That is an inference from `Reader::fill`, which explains why it ran at 7.25 s where `Framed::open` took 12.70 s.

On the Ryzen 7 9800X3D with a Samsung 990 PRO, 64 KiB and 1 MiB reads took the same time cold, and 1 MiB was no slower warm.

## Proposal

Raise `index::CHUNK` from 64 KiB to 1 MiB, and `lines::CHUNK` with it, since `lines.rs` keeps the two equal on purpose. That sets the read size for `build_index`, for `line_index`, and for a new `Reader`'s first buffer. Expected on this server: `Framed::open` cold from 12.7 s to about 6.6 s. 8 MiB was slower than 1 MiB, so 1 MiB is the size to try first.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/0eeac819
notes.text:
The change, run on the server by the sufr session: `index::CHUNK` and `lines::CHUNK` at 1 MiB against libsail 0.4.3, on the same 19.46 GB file, cold, 3 runs each in one sitting. Times are medians in seconds.

| variant | 0.4.3, 64 KiB | 1 MiB |
|---|---|---|
| `Framed::open` | 12.81 | 6.52 |
| `index::Reader`, whole file | 7.23 | 7.15 |
| 1 range | 7.22 | 7.15 |
| 4 ranges | 5.69 | 5.76 |

`Framed::open` now reads as fast as one `dd` stream (6.48 s). The others did not change, as expected, since `Reader` already read in large pieces. Another user's load rose during the 0.4.3 half, and those numbers still matched the first probe within a few percent. On the Ryzen 7 9800X3D with a Samsung 990 PRO, the change measured within 5% warm and cold, inside run-to-run spread.
